1	# obsd
2	
3	Minimal, dependency-free backend skeleton for **metrics ingestion, alerting and
4	SLO tracking**. Python 3.10+, standard library only, offline, deterministic
5	(every time-dependent entry point takes an injected `now_ms`).
6	
7	The lane goal is a metrics collection, alerting and SLO backend that grows
8	towards time-series writes and downsampling, label indexing and a query subset,
9	aggregation and sliding windows, alert rules with silencing and inhibition,
10	notification routing and dedup, SLO and error-budget math, retention and
11	compaction, multi-tenant quota, access control and audit, and consistent reads
12	under high availability. This seed implements the first, smallest *real* slice of
13	each of those areas.
14	
15	## Run
16	
17	```bash
18	# HTTP API (data dir flag is global and comes BEFORE the subcommand)
19	python3 -m obsd --data-dir ./obsd_data serve --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080
20	
21	# test suite
22	python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -v
23	```
24	
25	Both commands are run offline with the system interpreter; no third-party
26	package is imported anywhere.
27	
28	## CLI
29	
30	`python3 -m obsd [--data-dir ./obsd_data] <command> ...` prints exactly one line
31	of JSON on stdout. On error it prints one line of JSON (`{"error":"..."}`) on
32	stderr and exits non-zero.
33	
34	| Command | Example |
35	| --- | --- |
36	| `serve` | `python3 -m obsd --data-dir ./obsd_data serve --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080` |
37	| `quota-set` | `python3 -m obsd quota-set --tenant acme --max-series 1000 --max-points 1000000` |
38	| `quota-get` | `python3 -m obsd quota-get --tenant acme` |
39	| `retention-set` | `python3 -m obsd retention-set --tenant acme --retention-ms 86400000` (omit `--retention-ms` for no cleanup) |
40	| `retention-get` | `python3 -m obsd retention-get --tenant acme` |
41	| `retention-run` | `python3 -m obsd retention-run --now-ms 2000 [--tenant acme] [--dry-run]` |
42	| `write` | `python3 -m obsd write --tenant acme --metric latency_ms --label host=a --sample 1000:12.5 --now-ms 2000` |
43	| `write-batch` | `python3 -m obsd write-batch --entries '[{"tenant":"acme","metric":"latency_ms","samples":[[1000,12.5]]}]' --now-ms 2000` |
44	| `query` | `python3 -m obsd query --tenant acme --metric latency_ms --start 0 --end 5000 --step 1000 --agg avg` |
45	| `query` (grouped) | `python3 -m obsd query --tenant acme --metric latency_ms --agg avg --group-by '["host"]'` |
46	| `query` (matchers) | `python3 -m obsd query --tenant acme --metric latency_ms --matchers '[{"key":"host","op":"=~","value":"api-.*"}]'` |
47	| `query` (sliding window) | `python3 -m obsd query --tenant acme --metric latency_ms --start 0 --end 5000 --step 1000 --window-ms 5000 --agg avg` |
48	| `export` | `python3 -m obsd export --tenant acme --metric latency_ms --start 0 --end 5000` |
49	| `replay` | `python3 -m obsd replay --snapshot '{"version":1,"snapshot_id":"...","entries":[...]}' --now-ms 5000` |
50	| `rule-add` | `python3 -m obsd rule-add --tenant acme --metric latency_ms --comparator "<" --threshold 10 --window-ms 60000 --for-ms 30000 --agg avg --severity warning` |
51	| `eval` | `python3 -m obsd eval --now-ms 68000` |
52	| `alerts` | `python3 -m obsd alerts --tenant acme --state firing` |
53	| `silence-add` | `python3 -m obsd silence-add --tenant acme --starts-ms 0 --ends-ms 90000 --reason maintenance` |
54	| `route-add` | `python3 -m obsd route-add --tenant acme --target pager --label host=a --severity critical --event firing --repeat-ms 300000` |
55	| `route-list` | `python3 -m obsd route-list --tenant acme` |
56	| `notification-list` | `python3 -m obsd notification-list --tenant acme --acked false` |
57	| `notification-ack` | `python3 -m obsd notification-ack --id notification-00001` |
58	| `slo set` | `python3 -m obsd slo set --tenant acme --name availability --metric latency_ms --good-comparator ">=" --threshold 1 --target-ratio 0.9 --window-ms 60000` |
59	| `slo status` | `python3 -m obsd slo status --name availability --now-ms 60000` |
60	| `principal-create` | `python3 -m obsd principal-create --id ops --token s3cret --role admin --tenant acme --tenant globex` |
61	| `principal-list` | `python3 -m obsd principal-list` |
62	| `principal-revoke` | `python3 -m obsd principal-revoke --id ops` |
63	
64	## HTTP API
65	
66	Errors are always JSON: `{"error":"..."}` with status 400 (bad request),
67	404 (unknown resource) or 409 (write conflict or quota exceeded).
68	
69	| Method | Path | Request | Response |
70	| --- | --- | --- | --- |
71	| GET | `/healthz` | – | `200 {"ok":true}` |
72	| POST | `/v1/series` | `{"tenant","metric","labels","samples":[[ts,value],...],"now_ms"?,"overwrite"?}` | `202 {"written":n,"duplicates":m,"series_id":"..."}`, `400` on malformed input or a non-boolean `now_ms`/`overwrite` (an explicit `null` `overwrite` is rejected, not treated as `false`), `409` on conflicting timestamp or quota exceeded |
73	| POST | `/v1/series/batch` | `{"entries":[{"tenant","metric","samples","labels"?},...],"now_ms"?,"overwrite"?}` | `202 {"written":n,"duplicates":m,"results":[{"series_id","written","duplicates"},...]}`, `400` on malformed entries, `409` on conflict or quota exceeded |
74	| GET | `/v1/query` | `?tenant=&metric=&label.k=v&start=&end=&step=&agg=&group_by=&window=&matchers=` (group_by and matchers are JSON arrays; matchers holds `{"key","op","value"}` objects) | `200 {"series":[{"labels":{...},"points":[[ts,value\|null],...]}]}` |
75	| GET | `/v1/export` | `?tenant=&metric=&label.k=v&start=&end=&matchers=` (same filters and closed-interval semantics as `/v1/query`) | `200 {"version":1,"snapshot_id":"...","entries":[{"tenant","metric","labels","samples"},...]}` |
76	| POST | `/v1/replay` | `{"version":1,"snapshot_id":"...","entries":[...],"now_ms"?,"overwrite"?,"dry_run"?}` | `202 {"written":n,"duplicates":m,"results":[...],"applied":true}` (`200` with `"applied":false` for a dry run), `400` on invalid input or digest mismatch, `409` on conflict or quota exceeded |
77	| POST | `/v1/quotas` | `{"tenant","max_series":n\|null,"max_points":n\|null}` | `200 {"tenant","max_series","max_points","series","points"}`; invalid tenant/limits give `400` and leave config untouched |
78	| GET | `/v1/quotas` | `?tenant=` | `200 {"tenant","max_series","max_points","series","points"}` (unconfigured tenant reports `null` limits and real usage) |
79	| POST | `/v1/retention/policies` | `{"tenant","retention_ms":n\|null}` | `200 {"tenant","retention_ms","series","points"}`; invalid tenant/policy or unknown fields give `400` and leave config untouched |
80	| GET | `/v1/retention/policies` | `?tenant=` | `200 {"tenant","retention_ms","series","points"}` (unconfigured tenant reports a `null` policy and real usage) |
81	| POST | `/v1/retention/run` | `{"now_ms":n,"tenant"?,"dry_run"?}` | `200 {"dry_run":b,"tenants":[{"tenant","cutoff_ms","dropped","affected_series","remaining_points","compacted_series"},...]}`; missing/non-integer `now_ms`, non-boolean `dry_run` or unknown fields give `400` |
82	| POST | `/v1/rules` | rule object | `201` stored rule |
83	| GET | `/v1/rules` | `?tenant=` | `200 {"rules":[...]}` |
84	| POST | `/v1/evaluate` | `{"now_ms":n}` | `200 {"firing":[...],"silenced":[...],"inhibited":[...],"resolved":[...]}` |
85	| GET | `/v1/alerts` | `?tenant=&state=` | `200 {"alerts":[...]}` |
86	| POST | `/v1/silences` | `{"tenant","labels","starts_ms","ends_ms","reason"}` | `201` stored silence |
87	| POST | `/v1/inhibitions` | `{"source_severity","target_severity","same_labels"?}` | `201` stored inhibition; `same_labels` must be a real boolean (omitted defaults to `true`; `null`, numbers and strings are rejected with `400` and change nothing) |
88	| POST | `/v1/notification-routes` | `{"tenant","target","labels"?,"severities"?,"events"?,"repeat_ms"?,"id"?}` | `201` stored route; `400` invalid, `409` duplicate id |
89	| GET | `/v1/notification-routes` | `?tenant=` | `200 {"routes":[...]}` |
90	| DELETE | `/v1/notification-routes/{id}` | – | `200 {"deleted":id}`; `404` unknown route (notifications are kept) |
91	| GET | `/v1/notifications` | `?tenant=&route_id=&alert_id=&acked=` | `200 {"notifications":[...]}` (read-only, never consumes) |
92	| POST | `/v1/notifications/{id}/ack` | – | `200` stored notification (re-ack returns the same record); `404` unknown notification |
93	| POST | `/v1/slos` | `{"tenant","name","metric","labels","good_comparator","threshold","target_ratio","window_ms"}` | `201` stored SLO |
94	| GET | `/v1/slos/status` | `?tenant=&name=&now_ms=` | `200` SLO status object |
95	| GET | `/v1/stats` | – | `200 {"store":{...},"alerts":n}` |
96	| GET | `/v1/audit` | `?tenant=&principal_id=&outcome=&after_seq=&limit=` | `200 {"entries":[{"seq","principal_id","method","path","tenant","outcome","status"},...]}` ascending by `seq` (admin only) |
97	
98	**Access control and audit.** Principals are managed locally through the CLI
99	(`principal-create`/`principal-list`/`principal-revoke`); a principal is a
100	unique `--id`, a non-empty `--token`, a `--role` of `viewer`, `writer` or
101	`admin`, and at least one `--tenant` scope. Only the token's SHA-256 digest is
102	persisted (`access.json`); the token itself never appears in any output,
103	listing or audit record. A duplicate id is a conflict (`409` semantics), an
104	unknown id on revoke is `unknown principal: ...` (`404` semantics). While no
105	`access.json` exists, access control is off: every request stays anonymous,
106	nothing returns `401`/`403`, no audit records are written and `/healthz` is
107	always public either way.
108	
109	Once the config exists, every non-`/healthz` request must carry
110	`Authorization: Bearer <token>`: a missing, malformed or unknown token gets
111	`401 {"error":"unauthorized"}`. An authenticated principal whose role or
112	tenant scope does not cover the request gets `403 {"error":"forbidden"}`.
113	`viewer` reads resources inside its tenant scope; `writer` additionally
114	writes series, manages rules, silences, routes and SLOs and acknowledges
115	notifications inside its scope; `admin` additionally runs quotas, inhibitions,
116	evaluation, stats and the audit endpoint, and is the only role allowed to run
117	cross-tenant operations (requests with no single tenant, such as an
118	unfiltered `GET /v1/alerts`). Batch writes are checked per entry: if any
119	entry's tenant is outside the caller's scope the whole batch is rejected with
120	`403` before anything is written, preserving atomicity. Principals created or
121	revoked through the CLI take effect on a running server without a restart.
122	
123	Every non-`/healthz` request — authentication rejections, authorization
124	denials and business failures included — appends one persistent audit record
125	to `audit.jsonl` with a monotonically increasing `seq`:
126	`{"seq","principal_id","method","path","tenant","outcome","status"}`, where
127	`principal_id` is `null` when the request could not be authenticated,
128	`tenant` is `null` when the request has no single tenant, and `outcome` is
129	`allowed` (authorized, status < 400), `denied` (`401`/`403`) or `failed`
130	(authorized but the business logic rejected it). The log is reloaded on
131	startup, so records and the `seq` sequence survive restarts.
132	`GET /v1/audit` (admin only) filters by `tenant`, `principal_id`, `outcome`
133	and `after_seq` (entries with `seq > after_seq`) and pages with a positive
134	integer `limit`; invalid filters are `400`, non-admin access is `403`.
135	
136	## Data model
137	
138	A series identity is `(tenant, metric, sorted(label pairs))`. The canonical
139	identity string joins the tenant, the metric and every `key=value` label pair
140	(sorted by key) with `\n`:
141	
142	```
143	acme\nlatency_ms\nhost=a\nregion=eu
144	```
145	
146	`series_id = sha256(canonical_identity).hexdigest()`, so the same logical series
147	always maps to the same 64-character id, independent of label insertion order.
148	
149	Storage layout (all writes atomic via temp file + `os.replace`):
150	
151	```
152	<data-dir>/series.json              registry: series_id -> tenant/metric/labels
153	<data-dir>/points/<series_id>.jsonl one {"t":ts,"v":value} object per line
154	<data-dir>/quotas.json              tenant -> {"max_series","max_points"} limits
155	<data-dir>/retention.json           tenant -> {"retention_ms"} retention policies
156	<data-dir>/rules.json               <data-dir>/alerts.json
157	<data-dir>/slos.json                <data-dir>/silences.json
158	<data-dir>/inhibitions.json         <data-dir>/counters.json
159	<data-dir>/routes.json              <data-dir>/notifications.json
160	<data-dir>/notify_state.json        per-(route, alert) notification dedup state
161	<data-dir>/access.json              principals: id, token SHA-256 digest, role, tenants
162	<data-dir>/audit.jsonl              one audit record per line, seq monotonically increasing
163	```
164	
165	A directory written before quotas existed simply has no `quotas.json`, which
166	means every tenant is unlimited; limits and usage are reloaded together on
167	construction so a reopen always reports a consistent snapshot.
168	
169	`SeriesStore` and `AlertEngine` each guard their state with a
170	`threading.RLock`, so the threaded HTTP server can serve concurrent requests; all
171	state is reloaded from disk on construction, so a restart preserves series,
172	points, rules, alerts, silences, inhibitions, SLOs, notification routes and
173	queued notifications.
174	
175	## Semantics and formulas
176	
177	**Idempotent write.** `write(tenant, metric, labels, samples, now=None,
178	overwrite=False)` stores `(timestamp_ms, value)` pairs. Writing an existing
179	`(series, timestamp)` with the *same* value is a duplicate: it changes nothing
180	and is counted in `duplicates`. A *different* value for a stored timestamp is a
181	conflict: it raises `ObsError` (`409` over HTTP) unless `overwrite=True`, in
182	which case the stored value is replaced and counted in `written`. A timestamp
183	greater than the injected `now` (when `now` is given) is rejected. `now` is
184	`None`/omitted (no future check) or a non-boolean integer; `overwrite` must be
185	a boolean (default `False`). Anything else raises `ObsError` (`400` over HTTP)
186	before any validation or state change: no series, points, write counter, quota
187	usage or temp file is touched.
188	
189	**Atomic multi-series write.** `write_batch(entries, now=None, overwrite=False)`
190	(also `POST /v1/series/batch` and the CLI `write-batch --entries '<json>'`)
191	applies a non-empty list of `{"tenant","metric","samples","labels"?}` entries
192	(`labels` omitted means `{}`, no other keys allowed) as one all-or-nothing
193	unit. Entries may span tenants and metrics and may repeat a series. `now` is
194	`null`/omitted (no future check) or a non-boolean integer; `overwrite` must be
195	a boolean (default `false`). The whole batch is validated before any conflict
196	is reported, and all conflicts before any quota check. Entries and their
197	samples are then applied in input order, so a later entry sees the earlier
198	entries of the same batch: a same-value restatement is a duplicate, a
199	differing value conflicts unless `overwrite` (then it replaces and counts as
200	written). The result is `{"written","duplicates","results"}` with one
201	`{"series_id","written","duplicates"}` per entry in input order; the totals
202	are the per-entry sums. A successful batch with `written > 0` increases
203	`stats()["writes"]` by exactly one; a pure-duplicate batch increases nothing.
204	Quotas are charged per tenant with the batch's net new series and distinct new
205	timestamps — duplicates and overwrites add no occupancy, and only dimensions
206	that actually increase are checked. Any rejection (structure, missing fields,
207	per-entry validation, future samples → `400`; conflict or quota → `409`)
208	leaves no series, sample or write-count change behind, on disk included, and
209	concurrent queries and quota reads only ever see the state before or after the
210	whole batch. Replaying the same batch re-judges duplicates and overwrites in
211	the same order.
212	
213	**Snapshot export and replay.** `export_snapshot(tenant, metric, labels=None,
214	start_ms=None, end_ms=None, matchers=None)` (also `GET /v1/export` and the CLI
215	`export`) captures the raw samples of every matching series as a verifiable
216	document `{"version": 1, "snapshot_id": ..., "entries": [...]}`. The filters
217	and the closed `[start_ms, end_ms]` interval behave exactly as in `query`.
218	Each entry holds only `tenant`, `metric`, `labels` and `samples` (ascending by
219	timestamp); entries are ordered by `series_id` and registered series with no
220	sample in range are omitted. `snapshot_id` is the SHA-256 of the sorted,
221	compact JSON UTF-8 bytes of `{"version": 1, "entries": [...]}`. The export
222	reads one coherent snapshot under a single lock acquisition and never changes
223	write counters, quotas, alerts or query results, so exporting the same state
224	twice yields identical content.
225	
226	`replay_snapshot(snapshot, now_ms=None, overwrite=False, dry_run=False)` (also
227	`POST /v1/replay` and the CLI `replay --snapshot '<json>'`) verifies the
228	document before storing anything: the version must be 1, `snapshot_id` must
229	match the entries digest, and every entry then goes through the `write_batch`
230	rules (labels, samples, future timestamps against `now_ms` when given,
231	conflicts, per-tenant quotas). Invalid input or a digest mismatch is a `400`,
232	a conflict or quota breach a `409`, and any failure leaves no in-memory or
233	on-disk change behind. The result is `{"written", "duplicates", "results",
234	"applied"}` with `results` in entry order. A dry run (`dry_run=true` /
235	`--dry-run`) performs all validation and counting but applies nothing and
236	reports `applied: false`; a real replay reports `applied: true` (`202` over
237	HTTP, `200` for a dry run). Replaying a snapshot onto the state it came from
238	is a pure duplicate replay (`written == 0`, the write counter does not move),
239	replaying onto a partial state fills in only the missing points, and a replay
240	after a restart re-judges exactly as an in-process one. Replay never mints new
241	series identities and does not alter labels, tenant isolation, query
242	aggregation, alert or SLO semantics. With access control enabled, export is a
243	`read` operation scoped to the requested tenant and replay is a `write`
244	operation checked per entry — any entry outside the caller's scope rejects the
245	whole replay with `403` — and both are audited like every other endpoint.
246	
247	**Bucketing.** `query(..., step_ms=step, agg=agg)` assigns a sample with
248	timestamp `t` to bucket `b = t - (t % step)`, i.e. buckets are
249	left-closed/right-open (`[b, b+step)`) on epoch multiples. Every bucket from the
250	first non-empty bucket to the last non-empty bucket that also lies inside
251	`[start_ms, end_ms]` is emitted, and buckets with no sample are emitted as
252	`[b, null]`. Bucket value = `agg` over the samples in the bucket, where `agg` is
253	one of `sum`, `avg`, `min`, `max`, `count`. A series whose range contains no
254	sample is still listed with an empty `points` list. With `agg` and *no*
255	`step_ms` the whole `[start_ms, end_ms]` range is a single bucket. With neither,
256	raw samples are returned in `[timestamp, value]` order. `rollup(tenant, metric,
257	labels, window_ms, agg)` is `query` with `step_ms = window_ms` over the whole
258	stored range, with empty buckets dropped; output is ordered by `series_id`, so
259	it is deterministic.
260	
261	**Label matchers.** In addition to exact `labels` / `label.k=v` filtering,
262	`query` accepts `matchers` (`matchers` on `GET /v1/query`, `--matchers` on the
263	CLI): a JSON array of objects containing exactly `key` (non-empty string),
264	`op` and `value` (string, may be empty). Ops are `=` / `!=` (exact whole-string
265	equality and negation) and `=~` / `!~` (Python `re` syntax matched against the
266	*whole* label value via full match, case-sensitive and Unicode-aware, and its
267	negation). Omitting the parameter, passing Python `None`, or sending `[]` adds
268	no condition; an explicit JSON `null` or empty text is rejected (HTTP/CLI).
269	Matchers combine with each other and with the exact label filters by logical
270	AND — including several matchers on the same key — apply to raw series labels
271	before bucketing or grouping (labels absent from `group_by` count too), and are
272	restricted to the requested `tenant` and `metric`; `tenant`, `metric` and
273	`series_id` are not implicit labels. A missing key never satisfies `=`/`=~` but
274	always satisfies `!=`/`!~`, so `=~ ""` selects only series where the key exists
275	with an empty value (grouping still separates a missing key from an empty
276	value). `api-.*` matches `api-a` but not `xapi-a`. Duplicate matchers never
277	duplicate series, matcher order is irrelevant, and contradictory matchers
278	yield an empty result. Invalid JSON, a non-array, non-object elements, missing
279	or extra fields, wrong types, an empty `key`, an unsupported `op` or an invalid
280	regex raise `ObsError` (`400` over HTTP, one JSON error line on stderr for the
281	CLI); every matcher is validated even when no candidate series exists.
282	
283	**Grouped query.** `query(..., agg=agg, group_by=[keys...])` aggregates *across*
284	series: matching series (same tenant/metric/label filters and `[start_ms,
285	end_ms]` range as above) are bucketed into groups by the values of the given
286	label keys, and the raw in-range samples of all series in a group are pooled
287	before `agg` is applied — samples from different series at the same timestamp
288	count individually. `group_by=[]` merges every matching series into one group.
289	Each result row carries only `labels` (the group keys actually present on the
290	group's series — a missing key and an empty-string value form different
291	groups) and `points`; rows are ordered lexicographically by their sorted label
292	pairs. Bucketing follows the same rules as the per-series query (epoch-aligned
293	left-closed buckets with `null` gaps, or a single point at the group's
294	earliest sample without `step_ms`). A group whose series have no sample in
295	range is still listed with empty `points`; no matching series at all yields an
296	empty `series` array. `group_by` must be a list of distinct non-empty strings
297	and requires `agg`; violations raise `ObsError` (`400` over HTTP, one JSON
298	error line on stderr for the CLI).
299	
300	**Sliding-window query.** `query(..., start_ms=start, end_ms=end, step_ms=step,
301	agg=agg, window_ms=window)` switches to a separate mode the moment `window_ms`
302	is supplied (it is optional in every binding: `window` on `GET /v1/query`,
303	`--window-ms` on the CLI). In this mode `start_ms`, `end_ms`, `step_ms` and
304	`agg` are all required; `start_ms` and `end_ms` must be integer milliseconds,
305	`step_ms` and `window_ms` positive integer milliseconds, and `end_ms >=
306	start_ms` (bools, fractions and missing/unknown values are rejected). Evaluation
307	times are `t = start + k*step` for `k = 0, 1, ...`, keeping only times
308	`t <= end`; the output point timestamp is the evaluation time itself. The step
309	need not divide the window and windows are never aligned to fixed buckets.
310	
311	Each evaluation aggregates the raw samples in the half-open interval
312	`(t - window_ms, t]`: the left edge is excluded (a sample exactly one window
313	length earlier does not count), the right edge included (a sample at `t`
314	does). `start_ms` only constrains the output grid — the first window at
315	`start` also reads history older than `start`; no window ever reads a sample
316	newer than its own evaluation time. The aggregation uses the same meanings as
317	bucketing (`sum`, `avg`, `min`, `max`, `count`), and a window containing no
318	sample emits `[t, null]` for *every* aggregation, including `count`.
319	
320	Every matching registered series is returned on the full time grid even when
321	all of its windows are empty; no matching series yields an empty `series`
322	array. The Python per-series rows keep `series_id`; HTTP and CLI keep the
323	existing result shape. With `group_by`, all raw samples of the group's series
324	that fall in each window are pooled before aggregating (samples sharing a
325	timestamp across series count individually, `avg` divides by the total sample
326	count), a missing group key and an empty-string value stay distinct groups,
327	and each group keeps the full grid, fully null when no sample ever falls in a
328	window. Group filtering, ordering and validation follow the ordinary grouped
329	rules. The whole query reads one coherent snapshot, so concurrent writes or
330	retention sweeps can never mix old and new data; queries never alter samples,
331	counters or configuration, and the same history gives identical results after
332	reopening the store. Omitting `window_ms` preserves the previous query
333	behaviour exactly — `rollup`, write idempotency/overwrite, quotas, alerts and
334	SLOs are unaffected.
335	
336	**Counter aggregates.** In sliding-window mode `agg` also accepts `increase`
337	and `rate` (query entries only — `rollup`, alert rules and SLOs still reject
338	them, and using them without `window_ms` fails the query). Each matching
339	series is treated as a counter: within `(t - window_ms, t]` the time-sorted
340	adjacent readings contribute their difference when non-decreasing, while a
341	drop is a counter reset contributing only the later reading; the first reading
342	contributes nothing. Only samples actually inside the window are used — no
343	boundary borrowing, interpolation or extrapolation by window length.
344	`increase` is the sum of those deltas, `rate` that sum divided by the seconds
345	between the window's first and last sample. A window with fewer than two
346	distinct sample timestamps emits `[t, null]`; unchanged readings emit `0`.
347	Grouped queries compute each series independently and sum the non-null
348	per-series results (never differencing across series); a group whose series
349	are all null at a time emits null there. Any matched sample that actually
350	falls into an output window and is negative or non-finite fails the whole
351	query (`ObsError`, HTTP `400`, CLI non-zero with a one-line JSON error);
352	samples outside every window or filtered out by labels/matchers are never
353	inspected, and parameters are validated even when no series matches.
354	
355	**Retention.** `enforce_retention(tenant, cutoff_ms)` removes every sample of
356	that tenant with `timestamp_millis < cutoff_ms` and rewrites the affected point
357	files. `stats()` returns `{"series","points","writes","tenants"}`.
358	
359	**Retention policies and runs.** `set_retention(tenant, retention_ms)`
360	persists the tenant's policy in `retention.json` (also `POST
361	/v1/retention/policies` and the CLI `retention-set`); `retention_ms` is a
362	non-negative integer or `null` (no cleanup), and `get_retention(tenant)`
363	(also `GET /v1/retention/policies` and `retention-get`) returns
364	`{"tenant","retention_ms","series","points"}` — the normalised policy plus the
365	tenant's real usage, with a `null` policy for unconfigured tenants.
366	`run_retention(now_ms, tenant=None, dry_run=False)` (also `POST
367	/v1/retention/run` and `retention-run`) applies the configured policies as of
368	the injected `now_ms` (a required non-boolean integer): with a `tenant` only
369	that tenant is processed, otherwise every configured tenant in lexicographic
370	order. For each tenant `cutoff_ms = now_ms - retention_ms` and only samples
371	with `timestamp_ms < cutoff_ms` are dropped — a sample exactly at the cutoff
372	is kept; a `null` policy reports a `null` cutoff and zero deletions. Affected
373	point files are rewritten in compacted form (one physical record per
374	timestamp, the final value winning, legacy duplicate lines collapsed), empty
375	series stay registered, and the freed points count against the tenant's quota
376	immediately. The result is `{"dry_run","tenants":[...]}` with a stable
377	tenant order and `{"tenant","cutoff_ms","dropped","affected_series",
378	"remaining_points","compacted_series"}` per tenant. The whole run is one
379	atomic step under the store lock, so concurrent queries, quota and stats reads
380	only ever see the complete state before or after it; `dry_run=true` reports
381	the same numbers without touching memory, files, quotas or the write counter.
382	Policies and sweep results survive a restart. With access control enabled,
383	reading a policy is a tenant-scoped `read`, setting a policy and running a
384	single-tenant sweep are tenant-scoped `write`s, a sweep across every
385	configured tenant is admin-only, and all of them are audited.
386	
387	**Per-tenant quotas.** `set_quota(tenant, max_series, max_points)` sets the
388	tenant-wide limits; each limit is a non-negative integer or `null` (omitted
389	fields over HTTP also mean `null`, i.e. unlimited), and `0` forbids adding any.
390	`get_quota(tenant)` returns
391	`{"tenant","max_series","max_points","series","points"}` — the configured
392	limits and the current usage in one snapshot. Configuring a quota never creates
393	a series, and an unconfigured tenant is unlimited. Limits apply to all of a
394	tenant's metrics together: `series` is the number of registered series and
395	`points` the total number of *distinct timestamps* across those series, not
396	physical point-file lines. Label order, same-value replays, overwritten points
397	and a timestamp repeated inside one batch add no occupancy.
398	
399	Every write path (`SeriesStore.write`/`write_batch`, `POST /v1/series` and
400	`/v1/series/batch`, the CLI `write`/`write-batch`) is
401	checked after the existing input validation and conflict rules, using the
402	batch's net increase: a batch is rejected (ObsError / HTTP `409` / CLI JSON
403	error with non-zero exit) when *either* dimension it increases would exceed its
404	limit, and the rejection leaves no new series, samples or write-count change.
405	Limits may be lowered below current usage; afterwards only the dimensions a
406	write actually increases are checked — an already-over-limit dimension blocks
407	nothing by itself, so pure duplicates and overwrites keep succeeding. Retention
408	frees the occupancy of deleted points, while empty series stay registered.
409	Overwrites rewrite the point file so one timestamp never occupies two lines; on
410	reopen, any duplicate timestamp lines (including those left by older builds)
411	collapse to the last value, so historical re-overwrites never double-count.
412	
413	**Rule shape.** `{"id","tenant","metric","labels","comparator" ∈ {">",">=","<",
414	"<=","==","!="},"threshold","for_ms","window_ms","agg","severity" ∈ {"info",
415	"warning","critical"},"annotations"}`. `add_rule` validates every field and
416	raises `ObsError` for anything malformed (`id` is generated when omitted).
417	
418	**Evaluation window.** Let `step = window_ms`, `t = now_ms` and
419	`bucket_start(t) = t - (t % step)`. The window is
420	`[bucket_start(t) - step, t]`, i.e. the current bucket plus the whole previous
421	bucket. The rule condition holds for a series when *every* non-empty bucket in
422	that window satisfies `comparator(value, threshold)` — one violating bucket
423	anywhere in the window stops the condition, and it keeps stopping it until that
424	bucket has left the window.
425	
426	**`for_ms`.** Let `run_start` be the timestamp of the first bucket of the
427	current unbroken run of satisfying buckets (a violating bucket resets the run).
428	The rule fires only when the condition holds *and*
429	`bucket_start(now_ms) - run_start >= for_ms`. With `for_ms = 0`, one satisfied
430	bucket is enough; with `for_ms = window_ms`, the current and the previous bucket
431	must both be satisfied. Before the hold time is reached the alert is recorded
432	with `firing = false` and appears in none of the four output lists.
433	
434	**Alert identity and dedup.** Alert identity is `(rule_id, series_id)`, distinct
435	from the alert id. The first time a condition holds an alert id
436	`alert-NNNNN` is minted for that identity and reused forever: re-evaluating an
437	unchanged condition returns the *same* `id` and increments `occurrences` (the
438	number of evaluations in which the condition held). `since_ms` is `run_start`,
439	not the evaluation time, so dedup does not depend on the wall clock.
440	
441	**Resolution.** When the condition stops holding, the alert's state becomes
442	`resolved`, `firing` becomes `false`, `resolved_ms` is set once, and the alert is
443	reported in the `resolved` list of that evaluation. If the same condition holds
444	again later, the *same alert id* is reused and `occurrences` keeps counting.
445	Because the condition covers the whole window, a series that produced one bad
446	bucket stays unresolved until that bucket has left the window.
447	
448	**Silence vs inhibition precedence.** A condition that holds and whose `for_ms`
449	is satisfied is first checked against active silences: a silence is active when
450	`starts_ms <= now_ms <= ends_ms`, the tenant matches and every silence label
451	matcher is present in the series labels. Inside an active silence the alert state
452	is `silenced` (it is *not* firing) and the silence id and reason are recorded.
453	Only if no silence matches is inhibition checked: an inhibition
454	`(source_severity, target_severity, same_labels)` marks a `target_severity` alert
455	as `inhibited` while an alert of at least `source_severity` is currently
456	`firing` in the same tenant with *exactly the same label set*. Silence therefore
457	wins over inhibition. A silenced or inhibited alert still counts its
458	`occurrences` and returns to `firing` as soon as the silence/inhibition no longer
459	applies. `list_alerts(state=None)` filters by `firing`, `silenced`, `inhibited`
460	or `resolved`.
461	
462	**Notification routing.** `add_route({"tenant","target","labels"?,"severities"?,
463	"events"?,"repeat_ms"?,"id"?})` registers a notification route; `tenant` and
464	`target` are required non-empty strings, `labels` is an exact label subset the
465	alert's series must contain, `severities` (default: all severities) and
466	`events` (default: `["firing","resolved"]`, the only two allowed values) are
467	non-empty arrays when given, and `repeat_ms` is `null` or a non-negative
468	integer. Invalid shapes raise `ObsError` (HTTP `400`), a duplicate `id` is a
469	conflict (HTTP `409`), an unknown route is `404`; without an `id` the route is
470	named `route-NNNN`. Deleting a route keeps its historical notifications.
471	
472	`evaluate(now_ms)` still returns only the four state lists, but every alert
473	transition also appends to the notification queue of each matching route
474	(tenant equal, route labels a subset of the series labels, alert severity in
475	`severities`): an alert that enters `firing` — the first time, or when
476	recovering from `silenced`/`inhibited` — produces one `firing` record; while
477	the same firing state continues a repeat is emitted only when `repeat_ms` is
478	set and that much time has passed since the route's last notification for the
479	alert; entering `resolved` produces exactly one `resolved` record. Pending
480	(`for_ms` not yet met), silenced and inhibited alerts never produce `firing`
481	records. Dedup is tracked per route, so routes notify independently. Each
482	record is `{"id": "notification-NNNNN","route_id","alert_id","tenant",
483	"target","event","created_ms","alert": <snapshot>,"acked": false}` and is
484	persisted across restarts together with the dedup state.
485	`list_notifications(tenant, route_id, alert_id, acked)` reads the queue
486	without consuming it; `ack_notification(id)` marks a record acknowledged,
487	returns the same record on a repeated ack and raises `ObsError` (HTTP `404`)
488	for an unknown id.
489	
490	**SLO and error budget.** `set_slo(tenant, name, metric, labels,
491	good_comparator, threshold, target_ratio, window_ms)` defines a good-events
492	ratio SLO. `slo_status(name, now_ms, tenant=None)` counts every stored sample of
493	the matching series inside `[now_ms - window_ms, now_ms]`:
494	
495	```
496	total          = number of samples in the window (nulls excluded)
497	good           = samples where compare(value, good_comparator, threshold)
498	bad            = total - good
499	ratio          = good / total                             (0.0 when total == 0)
500	error_budget   = max(0.0, 1 - (1 - ratio) / (1 - target_ratio))   (target_ratio < 1)
501	               = 1.0 if ratio >= 1.0 else 0.0              (target_ratio == 1)
502	burn_rate      = (bad / total) / (1 - target_ratio)        (0.0 when target_ratio >= 1 or total == 0)
503	met            = ratio >= target_ratio
504	```
505	
506	`ratio` is the observed good ratio, `target_ratio ∈ (0,1]` the objective,
507	`burn_rate` how fast the budget is being spent relative to the allowed bad rate
508	(`1.0` means exactly on budget, `> 1.0` means burning too fast) and
509	`error_budget` the *fraction of the allowed error budget still unspent*:
510	`1.0` means untouched, `0.0` means exhausted or exceeded. For any `ratio` that
511	meets the target the two written forms of `error_budget` are identical, since
512	`1 - (1-ratio)/(1-target) = (ratio - target)/(1 - target)` and
513	`1 - ratio/target = (target - ratio)/target` are both non-negative only inside
514	their own regime; the first form is the one used, because it degrades sensibly
515	when the ratio beats the target (more budget left) instead of pinning to `0`.
516	With `total == 0` the ratio is `0.0`, so the budget counts as exhausted.
517	
518	Examples: 9 good + 1 bad with `target_ratio = 0.9` gives `ratio = 0.9`,
519	`error_budget = 0.0`, `burn_rate = 0.1/0.1 = 1.0`, `met = true` (exactly on
520	budget). 98 good + 2 bad with `target_ratio = 0.95` gives `ratio = 0.98`,
521	`burn_rate = 0.02/0.05 = 0.4` and `error_budget = 1 - 0.02/0.05 = 0.6` (60% of
522	the budget still unspent). 90 good + 10 bad with `target_ratio = 0.99` gives
523	`ratio = 0.9`, `burn_rate = 10.0`, `error_budget = 0.0`, `met = false`.
524	
525	**Determinism.** No module calls `time.time()` inside decision logic: `now_ms` is
526	passed into `evaluate`, `slo_status` and `write` (the HTTP layer uses the wall
527	clock only when a caller omits `now_ms` on `GET /v1/slos/status`, and
528	`/v1/slos/status` requires it in the CLI).
529	
530	## Layout
531	
532	```
533	obsd/__init__.py    public exports
534	obsd/tsdb.py        SeriesStore
535	obsd/alerts.py      AlertEngine
536	obsd/access.py      AccessControl (principals + audit log)
537	obsd/http_app.py    ThreadingHTTPServer + create_server
538	obsd/cli.py         command line interface
539	obsd/__main__.py    python3 -m obsd entry point
540	tests/              unittest suite (tsdb, alerts, http, access)
541	```
542	
543	## Tests
544	
545	```bash
546	python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -v
547	```
548	
549	Covered: series identity and label-order independence, idempotent re-write,
550	conflicting-timestamp rejection and `overwrite`, range filtering, epoch-aligned
551	buckets, null buckets, all five aggregations, deterministic rollups,
552	sliding-window grids with left-open/right-closed windows, null empty windows
553	(including count), full grids for empty series and groups, window argument
554	validation across Python/HTTP/CLI, window snapshot consistency under
555	concurrent writes and retention, retention,
556	restart safety, rule validation, `for_ms` timing, dedup with occurrence
557	counting, resolution and re-firing (including the window that keeps a bad bucket
558	blocking), silence scoping and expiry, inhibition by severity and exact label
559	set, SLO/error-budget/burn-rate math (including the empty window), quota
560	configuration/validation, net-increase enforcement and whole-batch rejection,
561	zero/lowered limits with duplicates and overwrites, tenant isolation, quota
562	release under retention, quota/usage consistency after reopen (including
563	collapsed duplicate timestamp lines), concurrent writes/reconfiguration/pruning,
564	retention policy set/get/validation and persistence, retention runs (exclusive
565	cutoff with the boundary point kept, lexicographic all-tenant sweeps, null
566	policies, dry runs without side effects, physical compaction of duplicate
567	timestamps, empty series staying registered, freed points reusable under quota,
568	restart-stable results, whole-state visibility under concurrent reads, and the
569	HTTP/CLI surfaces with tenant-scoped and admin-only access plus audit),
570	atomic multi-series batches (cross-tenant/cross-metric entries, in-batch
571	duplicate/overwrite ordering, all-or-nothing rejection on disk, per-tenant net
572	quota accounting, single write-count increment, and the HTTP/CLI surfaces),
573	principal create/list/revoke with digest-only token persistence, role and
574	tenant-scope enforcement (`401`/`403`) with the anonymous surface unchanged
575	while access control is off, per-entry batch authorization with atomic
576	rejection, the persistent audit log (seq monotonic across restarts, filters
577	and `limit` pagination on `GET /v1/audit`),
578	verifiable snapshot export (filters, ordering, digest, side-effect-free
579	repeatability across restarts) and replay (roundtrip migration, duplicate and
580	missing-point re-judgement, dry runs, digest/validation/conflict/quota
581	rejection without a trace, per-entry authorization, and the HTTP/CLI
582	surfaces),
583	and the live HTTP surface over a real socket.
584	
585	Everything is deterministic: the suite injects every timestamp it uses, and the
586	modules never read the wall clock inside decision logic.
587

# obsd

Minimal, dependency-free backend skeleton for **metrics ingestion, alerting and
SLO tracking**. Python 3.10+, standard library only, offline, deterministic
(every time-dependent entry point takes an injected `now_ms`).

The lane goal is a metrics collection, alerting and SLO backend that grows
towards time-series writes and downsampling, label indexing and a query subset,
aggregation and sliding windows, alert rules with silencing and inhibition,
notification routing and dedup, SLO and error-budget math, retention and
compaction, multi-tenant quota, access control and audit, and consistent reads
under high availability. This seed implements the first, smallest *real* slice of
each of those areas.

## Run

```bash
# HTTP API (data dir flag is global and comes BEFORE the subcommand)
python3 -m obsd --data-dir ./obsd_data serve --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080

# test suite
python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -v
```

Both commands are run offline with the system interpreter; no third-party
package is imported anywhere.

## CLI

`python3 -m obsd [--data-dir ./obsd_data] <command> ...` prints exactly one line
of JSON on stdout. On error it prints one line of JSON (`{"error":"..."}`) on
stderr and exits non-zero.

| Command | Example |
| --- | --- |
| `serve` | `python3 -m obsd --data-dir ./obsd_data serve --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080` |
| `quota-set` | `python3 -m obsd quota-set --tenant acme --max-series 1000 --max-points 1000000` |
| `quota-get` | `python3 -m obsd quota-get --tenant acme` |
| `retention-set` | `python3 -m obsd retention-set --tenant acme --retention-ms 86400000` (omit `--retention-ms` for no cleanup) |
| `retention-get` | `python3 -m obsd retention-get --tenant acme` |
| `retention-run` | `python3 -m obsd retention-run --now-ms 2000 [--tenant acme] [--dry-run]` |
| `write` | `python3 -m obsd write --tenant acme --metric latency_ms --label host=a --sample 1000:12.5 --now-ms 2000` |
| `write-batch` | `python3 -m obsd write-batch --entries '[{"tenant":"acme","metric":"latency_ms","samples":[[1000,12.5]]}]' --now-ms 2000` |
| `query` | `python3 -m obsd query --tenant acme --metric latency_ms --start 0 --end 5000 --step 1000 --agg avg` |
| `query` (grouped) | `python3 -m obsd query --tenant acme --metric latency_ms --agg avg --group-by '["host"]'` |
| `query` (matchers) | `python3 -m obsd query --tenant acme --metric latency_ms --matchers '[{"key":"host","op":"=~","value":"api-.*"}]'` |
| `query` (sliding window) | `python3 -m obsd query --tenant acme --metric latency_ms --start 0 --end 5000 --step 1000 --window-ms 5000 --agg avg` |
| `export` | `python3 -m obsd export --tenant acme --metric latency_ms --start 0 --end 5000` |
| `replay` | `python3 -m obsd replay --snapshot '{"version":1,"snapshot_id":"...","entries":[...]}' --now-ms 5000` |
| `rule-add` | `python3 -m obsd rule-add --tenant acme --metric latency_ms --comparator "<" --threshold 10 --window-ms 60000 --for-ms 30000 --agg avg --severity warning` |
| `eval` | `python3 -m obsd eval --now-ms 68000` |
| `alerts` | `python3 -m obsd alerts --tenant acme --state firing` |
| `silence-add` | `python3 -m obsd silence-add --tenant acme --starts-ms 0 --ends-ms 90000 --reason maintenance` |
| `route-add` | `python3 -m obsd route-add --tenant acme --target pager --label host=a --severity critical --event firing --repeat-ms 300000` |
| `route-list` | `python3 -m obsd route-list --tenant acme` |
| `notification-list` | `python3 -m obsd notification-list --tenant acme --acked false` |
| `notification-ack` | `python3 -m obsd notification-ack --id notification-00001` |
| `slo set` | `python3 -m obsd slo set --tenant acme --name availability --metric latency_ms --good-comparator ">=" --threshold 1 --target-ratio 0.9 --window-ms 60000` |
| `slo status` | `python3 -m obsd slo status --name availability --now-ms 60000` |
| `principal-create` | `python3 -m obsd principal-create --id ops --token s3cret --role admin --tenant acme --tenant globex` |
| `principal-list` | `python3 -m obsd principal-list` |
| `principal-revoke` | `python3 -m obsd principal-revoke --id ops` |

## HTTP API

Errors are always JSON: `{"error":"..."}` with status 400 (bad request),
404 (unknown resource) or 409 (write conflict or quota exceeded).

| Method | Path | Request | Response |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| GET | `/healthz` | – | `200 {"ok":true}` |
| POST | `/v1/series` | `{"tenant","metric","labels","samples":[[ts,value],...],"now_ms"?,"overwrite"?}` | `202 {"written":n,"duplicates":m,"series_id":"..."}`, `400` on malformed input or a non-boolean `now_ms`/`overwrite` (an explicit `null` `overwrite` is rejected, not treated as `false`), `409` on conflicting timestamp or quota exceeded |
| POST | `/v1/series/batch` | `{"entries":[{"tenant","metric","samples","labels"?},...],"now_ms"?,"overwrite"?}` | `202 {"written":n,"duplicates":m,"results":[{"series_id","written","duplicates"},...]}`, `400` on malformed entries, `409` on conflict or quota exceeded |
| GET | `/v1/query` | `?tenant=&metric=&label.k=v&start=&end=&step=&agg=&group_by=&window=&matchers=` (group_by and matchers are JSON arrays; matchers holds `{"key","op","value"}` objects) | `200 {"series":[{"labels":{...},"points":[[ts,value\|null],...]}]}` |
| GET | `/v1/export` | `?tenant=&metric=&label.k=v&start=&end=&matchers=` (same filters and closed-interval semantics as `/v1/query`) | `200 {"version":1,"snapshot_id":"...","entries":[{"tenant","metric","labels","samples"},...]}` |
| POST | `/v1/replay` | `{"version":1,"snapshot_id":"...","entries":[...],"now_ms"?,"overwrite"?,"dry_run"?}` | `202 {"written":n,"duplicates":m,"results":[...],"applied":true}` (`200` with `"applied":false` for a dry run), `400` on invalid input or digest mismatch, `409` on conflict or quota exceeded |
| POST | `/v1/quotas` | `{"tenant","max_series":n\|null,"max_points":n\|null}` | `200 {"tenant","max_series","max_points","series","points"}`; invalid tenant/limits give `400` and leave config untouched |
| GET | `/v1/quotas` | `?tenant=` | `200 {"tenant","max_series","max_points","series","points"}` (unconfigured tenant reports `null` limits and real usage) |
| POST | `/v1/retention/policies` | `{"tenant","retention_ms":n\|null}` | `200 {"tenant","retention_ms","series","points"}`; invalid tenant/policy or unknown fields give `400` and leave config untouched |
| GET | `/v1/retention/policies` | `?tenant=` | `200 {"tenant","retention_ms","series","points"}` (unconfigured tenant reports a `null` policy and real usage) |
| POST | `/v1/retention/run` | `{"now_ms":n,"tenant"?,"dry_run"?}` | `200 {"dry_run":b,"tenants":[{"tenant","cutoff_ms","dropped","affected_series","remaining_points","compacted_series"},...]}`; missing/non-integer `now_ms`, non-boolean `dry_run` or unknown fields give `400` |
| POST | `/v1/rules` | rule object | `201` stored rule |
| GET | `/v1/rules` | `?tenant=` | `200 {"rules":[...]}` |
| POST | `/v1/evaluate` | `{"now_ms":n}` | `200 {"firing":[...],"silenced":[...],"inhibited":[...],"resolved":[...]}` |
| GET | `/v1/alerts` | `?tenant=&state=` | `200 {"alerts":[...]}` |
| POST | `/v1/silences` | `{"tenant","labels","starts_ms","ends_ms","reason"}` | `201` stored silence |
| POST | `/v1/inhibitions` | `{"source_severity","target_severity","same_labels"?}` | `201` stored inhibition; `same_labels` must be a real boolean (omitted defaults to `true`; `null`, numbers and strings are rejected with `400` and change nothing) |
| POST | `/v1/notification-routes` | `{"tenant","target","labels"?,"severities"?,"events"?,"repeat_ms"?,"id"?}` | `201` stored route; `400` invalid, `409` duplicate id |
| GET | `/v1/notification-routes` | `?tenant=` | `200 {"routes":[...]}` |
| DELETE | `/v1/notification-routes/{id}` | – | `200 {"deleted":id}`; `404` unknown route (notifications are kept) |
| GET | `/v1/notifications` | `?tenant=&route_id=&alert_id=&acked=` | `200 {"notifications":[...]}` (read-only, never consumes) |
| POST | `/v1/notifications/{id}/ack` | – | `200` stored notification (re-ack returns the same record); `404` unknown notification |
| POST | `/v1/slos` | `{"tenant","name","metric","labels","good_comparator","threshold","target_ratio","window_ms"}` | `201` stored SLO |
| GET | `/v1/slos/status` | `?tenant=&name=&now_ms=` | `200` SLO status object |
| GET | `/v1/stats` | – | `200 {"store":{...},"alerts":n}` |
| GET | `/v1/audit` | `?tenant=&principal_id=&outcome=&after_seq=&limit=` | `200 {"entries":[{"seq","principal_id","method","path","tenant","outcome","status"},...]}` ascending by `seq` (admin only) |

**Access control and audit.** Principals are managed locally through the CLI
(`principal-create`/`principal-list`/`principal-revoke`); a principal is a
unique `--id`, a non-empty `--token`, a `--role` of `viewer`, `writer` or
`admin`, and at least one `--tenant` scope. Only the token's SHA-256 digest is
persisted (`access.json`); the token itself never appears in any output,
listing or audit record. A duplicate id is a conflict (`409` semantics), an
unknown id on revoke is `unknown principal: ...` (`404` semantics). While no
`access.json` exists, access control is off: every request stays anonymous,
nothing returns `401`/`403`, no audit records are written and `/healthz` is
always public either way.

Once the config exists, every non-`/healthz` request must carry
`Authorization: Bearer <token>`: a missing, malformed or unknown token gets
`401 {"error":"unauthorized"}`. An authenticated principal whose role or
tenant scope does not cover the request gets `403 {"error":"forbidden"}`.
`viewer` reads resources inside its tenant scope; `writer` additionally
writes series, manages rules, silences, routes and SLOs and acknowledges
notifications inside its scope; `admin` additionally runs quotas, inhibitions,
evaluation, stats and the audit endpoint, and is the only role allowed to run
cross-tenant operations (requests with no single tenant, such as an
unfiltered `GET /v1/alerts`). Batch writes are checked per entry: if any
entry's tenant is outside the caller's scope the whole batch is rejected with
`403` before anything is written, preserving atomicity. Principals created or
revoked through the CLI take effect on a running server without a restart.

Every non-`/healthz` request — authentication rejections, authorization
denials and business failures included — appends one persistent audit record
to `audit.jsonl` with a monotonically increasing `seq`:
`{"seq","principal_id","method","path","tenant","outcome","status"}`, where
`principal_id` is `null` when the request could not be authenticated,
`tenant` is `null` when the request has no single tenant, and `outcome` is
`allowed` (authorized, status < 400), `denied` (`401`/`403`) or `failed`
(authorized but the business logic rejected it). The log is reloaded on
startup, so records and the `seq` sequence survive restarts.
`GET /v1/audit` (admin only) filters by `tenant`, `principal_id`, `outcome`
and `after_seq` (entries with `seq > after_seq`) and pages with a positive
integer `limit`; invalid filters are `400`, non-admin access is `403`.

## Data model

A series identity is `(tenant, metric, sorted(label pairs))`. The canonical
identity string joins the tenant, the metric and every `key=value` label pair
(sorted by key) with `\n`:

```
acme\nlatency_ms\nhost=a\nregion=eu
```

`series_id = sha256(canonical_identity).hexdigest()`, so the same logical series
always maps to the same 64-character id, independent of label insertion order.

Storage layout (all writes atomic via temp file + `os.replace`):

```
<data-dir>/series.json              registry: series_id -> tenant/metric/labels
<data-dir>/points/<series_id>.jsonl one {"t":ts,"v":value} object per line
<data-dir>/quotas.json              tenant -> {"max_series","max_points"} limits
<data-dir>/retention.json           tenant -> {"retention_ms"} retention policies
<data-dir>/rules.json               <data-dir>/alerts.json
<data-dir>/slos.json                <data-dir>/silences.json
<data-dir>/inhibitions.json         <data-dir>/counters.json
<data-dir>/routes.json              <data-dir>/notifications.json
<data-dir>/notify_state.json        per-(route, alert) notification dedup state
<data-dir>/access.json              principals: id, token SHA-256 digest, role, tenants
<data-dir>/audit.jsonl              one audit record per line, seq monotonically increasing
```

A directory written before quotas existed simply has no `quotas.json`, which
means every tenant is unlimited; limits and usage are reloaded together on
construction so a reopen always reports a consistent snapshot.

`SeriesStore` and `AlertEngine` each guard their state with a
`threading.RLock`, so the threaded HTTP server can serve concurrent requests; all
state is reloaded from disk on construction, so a restart preserves series,
points, rules, alerts, silences, inhibitions, SLOs, notification routes and
queued notifications.

## Semantics and formulas

**Idempotent write.** `write(tenant, metric, labels, samples, now=None,
overwrite=False)` stores `(timestamp_ms, value)` pairs. Writing an existing
`(series, timestamp)` with the *same* value is a duplicate: it changes nothing
and is counted in `duplicates`. A *different* value for a stored timestamp is a
conflict: it raises `ObsError` (`409` over HTTP) unless `overwrite=True`, in
which case the stored value is replaced and counted in `written`. A timestamp
greater than the injected `now` (when `now` is given) is rejected. `now` is
`None`/omitted (no future check) or a non-boolean integer; `overwrite` must be
a boolean (default `False`). Anything else raises `ObsError` (`400` over HTTP)
before any validation or state change: no series, points, write counter, quota
usage or temp file is touched.

**Atomic multi-series write.** `write_batch(entries, now=None, overwrite=False)`
(also `POST /v1/series/batch` and the CLI `write-batch --entries '<json>'`)
applies a non-empty list of `{"tenant","metric","samples","labels"?}` entries
(`labels` omitted means `{}`, no other keys allowed) as one all-or-nothing
unit. Entries may span tenants and metrics and may repeat a series. `now` is
`null`/omitted (no future check) or a non-boolean integer; `overwrite` must be
a boolean (default `false`). The whole batch is validated before any conflict
is reported, and all conflicts before any quota check. Entries and their
samples are then applied in input order, so a later entry sees the earlier
entries of the same batch: a same-value restatement is a duplicate, a
differing value conflicts unless `overwrite` (then it replaces and counts as
written). The result is `{"written","duplicates","results"}` with one
`{"series_id","written","duplicates"}` per entry in input order; the totals
are the per-entry sums. A successful batch with `written > 0` increases
`stats()["writes"]` by exactly one; a pure-duplicate batch increases nothing.
Quotas are charged per tenant with the batch's net new series and distinct new
timestamps — duplicates and overwrites add no occupancy, and only dimensions
that actually increase are checked. Any rejection (structure, missing fields,
per-entry validation, future samples → `400`; conflict or quota → `409`)
leaves no series, sample or write-count change behind, on disk included, and
concurrent queries and quota reads only ever see the state before or after the
whole batch. Replaying the same batch re-judges duplicates and overwrites in
the same order.

**Snapshot export and replay.** `export_snapshot(tenant, metric, labels=None,
start_ms=None, end_ms=None, matchers=None)` (also `GET /v1/export` and the CLI
`export`) captures the raw samples of every matching series as a verifiable
document `{"version": 1, "snapshot_id": ..., "entries": [...]}`. The filters
and the closed `[start_ms, end_ms]` interval behave exactly as in `query`.
Each entry holds only `tenant`, `metric`, `labels` and `samples` (ascending by
timestamp); entries are ordered by `series_id` and registered series with no
sample in range are omitted. `snapshot_id` is the SHA-256 of the sorted,
compact JSON UTF-8 bytes of `{"version": 1, "entries": [...]}`. The export
reads one coherent snapshot under a single lock acquisition and never changes
write counters, quotas, alerts or query results, so exporting the same state
twice yields identical content.

`replay_snapshot(snapshot, now_ms=None, overwrite=False, dry_run=False)` (also
`POST /v1/replay` and the CLI `replay --snapshot '<json>'`) verifies the
document before storing anything: the version must be 1, `snapshot_id` must
match the entries digest, and every entry then goes through the `write_batch`
rules (labels, samples, future timestamps against `now_ms` when given,
conflicts, per-tenant quotas). Invalid input or a digest mismatch is a `400`,
a conflict or quota breach a `409`, and any failure leaves no in-memory or
on-disk change behind. The result is `{"written", "duplicates", "results",
"applied"}` with `results` in entry order. A dry run (`dry_run=true` /
`--dry-run`) performs all validation and counting but applies nothing and
reports `applied: false`; a real replay reports `applied: true` (`202` over
HTTP, `200` for a dry run). Replaying a snapshot onto the state it came from
is a pure duplicate replay (`written == 0`, the write counter does not move),
replaying onto a partial state fills in only the missing points, and a replay
after a restart re-judges exactly as an in-process one. Replay never mints new
series identities and does not alter labels, tenant isolation, query
aggregation, alert or SLO semantics. With access control enabled, export is a
`read` operation scoped to the requested tenant and replay is a `write`
operation checked per entry — any entry outside the caller's scope rejects the
whole replay with `403` — and both are audited like every other endpoint.

**Bucketing.** `query(..., step_ms=step, agg=agg)` assigns a sample with
timestamp `t` to bucket `b = t - (t % step)`, i.e. buckets are
left-closed/right-open (`[b, b+step)`) on epoch multiples. Every bucket from the
first non-empty bucket to the last non-empty bucket that also lies inside
`[start_ms, end_ms]` is emitted, and buckets with no sample are emitted as
`[b, null]`. Bucket value = `agg` over the samples in the bucket, where `agg` is
one of `sum`, `avg`, `min`, `max`, `count`. A series whose range contains no
sample is still listed with an empty `points` list. With `agg` and *no*
`step_ms` the whole `[start_ms, end_ms]` range is a single bucket. With neither,
raw samples are returned in `[timestamp, value]` order. `rollup(tenant, metric,
labels, window_ms, agg)` is `query` with `step_ms = window_ms` over the whole
stored range, with empty buckets dropped; output is ordered by `series_id`, so
it is deterministic.

**Label matchers.** In addition to exact `labels` / `label.k=v` filtering,
`query` accepts `matchers` (`matchers` on `GET /v1/query`, `--matchers` on the
CLI): a JSON array of objects containing exactly `key` (non-empty string),
`op` and `value` (string, may be empty). Ops are `=` / `!=` (exact whole-string
equality and negation) and `=~` / `!~` (Python `re` syntax matched against the
*whole* label value via full match, case-sensitive and Unicode-aware, and its
negation). Omitting the parameter, passing Python `None`, or sending `[]` adds
no condition; an explicit JSON `null` or empty text is rejected (HTTP/CLI).
Matchers combine with each other and with the exact label filters by logical
AND — including several matchers on the same key — apply to raw series labels
before bucketing or grouping (labels absent from `group_by` count too), and are
restricted to the requested `tenant` and `metric`; `tenant`, `metric` and
`series_id` are not implicit labels. A missing key never satisfies `=`/`=~` but
always satisfies `!=`/`!~`, so `=~ ""` selects only series where the key exists
with an empty value (grouping still separates a missing key from an empty
value). `api-.*` matches `api-a` but not `xapi-a`. Duplicate matchers never
duplicate series, matcher order is irrelevant, and contradictory matchers
yield an empty result. Invalid JSON, a non-array, non-object elements, missing
or extra fields, wrong types, an empty `key`, an unsupported `op` or an invalid
regex raise `ObsError` (`400` over HTTP, one JSON error line on stderr for the
CLI); every matcher is validated even when no candidate series exists.

**Grouped query.** `query(..., agg=agg, group_by=[keys...])` aggregates *across*
series: matching series (same tenant/metric/label filters and `[start_ms,
end_ms]` range as above) are bucketed into groups by the values of the given
label keys, and the raw in-range samples of all series in a group are pooled
before `agg` is applied — samples from different series at the same timestamp
count individually. `group_by=[]` merges every matching series into one group.
Each result row carries only `labels` (the group keys actually present on the
group's series — a missing key and an empty-string value form different
groups) and `points`; rows are ordered lexicographically by their sorted label
pairs. Bucketing follows the same rules as the per-series query (epoch-aligned
left-closed buckets with `null` gaps, or a single point at the group's
earliest sample without `step_ms`). A group whose series have no sample in
range is still listed with empty `points`; no matching series at all yields an
empty `series` array. `group_by` must be a list of distinct non-empty strings
and requires `agg`; violations raise `ObsError` (`400` over HTTP, one JSON
error line on stderr for the CLI).

**Sliding-window query.** `query(..., start_ms=start, end_ms=end, step_ms=step,
agg=agg, window_ms=window)` switches to a separate mode the moment `window_ms`
is supplied (it is optional in every binding: `window` on `GET /v1/query`,
`--window-ms` on the CLI). In this mode `start_ms`, `end_ms`, `step_ms` and
`agg` are all required; `start_ms` and `end_ms` must be integer milliseconds,
`step_ms` and `window_ms` positive integer milliseconds, and `end_ms >=
start_ms` (bools, fractions and missing/unknown values are rejected). Evaluation
times are `t = start + k*step` for `k = 0, 1, ...`, keeping only times
`t <= end`; the output point timestamp is the evaluation time itself. The step
need not divide the window and windows are never aligned to fixed buckets.

Each evaluation aggregates the raw samples in the half-open interval
`(t - window_ms, t]`: the left edge is excluded (a sample exactly one window
length earlier does not count), the right edge included (a sample at `t`
does). `start_ms` only constrains the output grid — the first window at
`start` also reads history older than `start`; no window ever reads a sample
newer than its own evaluation time. The aggregation uses the same meanings as
bucketing (`sum`, `avg`, `min`, `max`, `count`), and a window containing no
sample emits `[t, null]` for *every* aggregation, including `count`.

Every matching registered series is returned on the full time grid even when
all of its windows are empty; no matching series yields an empty `series`
array. The Python per-series rows keep `series_id`; HTTP and CLI keep the
existing result shape. With `group_by`, all raw samples of the group's series
that fall in each window are pooled before aggregating (samples sharing a
timestamp across series count individually, `avg` divides by the total sample
count), a missing group key and an empty-string value stay distinct groups,
and each group keeps the full grid, fully null when no sample ever falls in a
window. Group filtering, ordering and validation follow the ordinary grouped
rules. The whole query reads one coherent snapshot, so concurrent writes or
retention sweeps can never mix old and new data; queries never alter samples,
counters or configuration, and the same history gives identical results after
reopening the store. Omitting `window_ms` preserves the previous query
behaviour exactly — `rollup`, write idempotency/overwrite, quotas, alerts and
SLOs are unaffected.

**Counter aggregates.** In sliding-window mode `agg` also accepts `increase`
and `rate` (query entries only — `rollup`, alert rules and SLOs still reject
them, and using them without `window_ms` fails the query). Each matching
series is treated as a counter: within `(t - window_ms, t]` the time-sorted
adjacent readings contribute their difference when non-decreasing, while a
drop is a counter reset contributing only the later reading; the first reading
contributes nothing. Only samples actually inside the window are used — no
boundary borrowing, interpolation or extrapolation by window length.
`increase` is the sum of those deltas, `rate` that sum divided by the seconds
between the window's first and last sample. A window with fewer than two
distinct sample timestamps emits `[t, null]`; unchanged readings emit `0`.
Grouped queries compute each series independently and sum the non-null
per-series results (never differencing across series); a group whose series
are all null at a time emits null there. Any matched sample that actually
falls into an output window and is negative or non-finite fails the whole
query (`ObsError`, HTTP `400`, CLI non-zero with a one-line JSON error);
samples outside every window or filtered out by labels/matchers are never
inspected, and parameters are validated even when no series matches.

**Retention.** `enforce_retention(tenant, cutoff_ms)` removes every sample of
that tenant with `timestamp_millis < cutoff_ms` and rewrites the affected point
files. `stats()` returns `{"series","points","writes","tenants"}`.

**Retention policies and runs.** `set_retention(tenant, retention_ms)`
persists the tenant's policy in `retention.json` (also `POST
/v1/retention/policies` and the CLI `retention-set`); `retention_ms` is a
non-negative integer or `null` (no cleanup), and `get_retention(tenant)`
(also `GET /v1/retention/policies` and `retention-get`) returns
`{"tenant","retention_ms","series","points"}` — the normalised policy plus the
tenant's real usage, with a `null` policy for unconfigured tenants.
`run_retention(now_ms, tenant=None, dry_run=False)` (also `POST
/v1/retention/run` and `retention-run`) applies the configured policies as of
the injected `now_ms` (a required non-boolean integer): with a `tenant` only
that tenant is processed, otherwise every configured tenant in lexicographic
order. For each tenant `cutoff_ms = now_ms - retention_ms` and only samples
with `timestamp_ms < cutoff_ms` are dropped — a sample exactly at the cutoff
is kept; a `null` policy reports a `null` cutoff and zero deletions. Affected
point files are rewritten in compacted form (one physical record per
timestamp, the final value winning, legacy duplicate lines collapsed), empty
series stay registered, and the freed points count against the tenant's quota
immediately. The result is `{"dry_run","tenants":[...]}` with a stable
tenant order and `{"tenant","cutoff_ms","dropped","affected_series",
"remaining_points","compacted_series"}` per tenant. The whole run is one
atomic step under the store lock, so concurrent queries, quota and stats reads
only ever see the complete state before or after it; `dry_run=true` reports
the same numbers without touching memory, files, quotas or the write counter.
Policies and sweep results survive a restart. With access control enabled,
reading a policy is a tenant-scoped `read`, setting a policy and running a
single-tenant sweep are tenant-scoped `write`s, a sweep across every
configured tenant is admin-only, and all of them are audited.

**Per-tenant quotas.** `set_quota(tenant, max_series, max_points)` sets the
tenant-wide limits; each limit is a non-negative integer or `null` (omitted
fields over HTTP also mean `null`, i.e. unlimited), and `0` forbids adding any.
`get_quota(tenant)` returns
`{"tenant","max_series","max_points","series","points"}` — the configured
limits and the current usage in one snapshot. Configuring a quota never creates
a series, and an unconfigured tenant is unlimited. Limits apply to all of a
tenant's metrics together: `series` is the number of registered series and
`points` the total number of *distinct timestamps* across those series, not
physical point-file lines. Label order, same-value replays, overwritten points
and a timestamp repeated inside one batch add no occupancy.

Every write path (`SeriesStore.write`/`write_batch`, `POST /v1/series` and
`/v1/series/batch`, the CLI `write`/`write-batch`) is
checked after the existing input validation and conflict rules, using the
batch's net increase: a batch is rejected (ObsError / HTTP `409` / CLI JSON
error with non-zero exit) when *either* dimension it increases would exceed its
limit, and the rejection leaves no new series, samples or write-count change.
Limits may be lowered below current usage; afterwards only the dimensions a
write actually increases are checked — an already-over-limit dimension blocks
nothing by itself, so pure duplicates and overwrites keep succeeding. Retention
frees the occupancy of deleted points, while empty series stay registered.
Overwrites rewrite the point file so one timestamp never occupies two lines; on
reopen, any duplicate timestamp lines (including those left by older builds)
collapse to the last value, so historical re-overwrites never double-count.

**Rule shape.** `{"id","tenant","metric","labels","comparator" ∈ {">",">=","<",
"<=","==","!="},"threshold","for_ms","window_ms","agg","severity" ∈ {"info",
"warning","critical"},"annotations"}`. `add_rule` validates every field and
raises `ObsError` for anything malformed (`id` is generated when omitted).

**Evaluation window.** Let `step = window_ms`, `t = now_ms` and
`bucket_start(t) = t - (t % step)`. The window is
`[bucket_start(t) - step, t]`, i.e. the current bucket plus the whole previous
bucket. The rule condition holds for a series when *every* non-empty bucket in
that window satisfies `comparator(value, threshold)` — one violating bucket
anywhere in the window stops the condition, and it keeps stopping it until that
bucket has left the window.

**`for_ms`.** Let `run_start` be the timestamp of the first bucket of the
current unbroken run of satisfying buckets (a violating bucket resets the run).
The rule fires only when the condition holds *and*
`bucket_start(now_ms) - run_start >= for_ms`. With `for_ms = 0`, one satisfied
bucket is enough; with `for_ms = window_ms`, the current and the previous bucket
must both be satisfied. Before the hold time is reached the alert is recorded
with `firing = false` and appears in none of the four output lists.

**Alert identity and dedup.** Alert identity is `(rule_id, series_id)`, distinct
from the alert id. The first time a condition holds an alert id
`alert-NNNNN` is minted for that identity and reused forever: re-evaluating an
unchanged condition returns the *same* `id` and increments `occurrences` (the
number of evaluations in which the condition held). `since_ms` is `run_start`,
not the evaluation time, so dedup does not depend on the wall clock.

**Resolution.** When the condition stops holding, the alert's state becomes
`resolved`, `firing` becomes `false`, `resolved_ms` is set once, and the alert is
reported in the `resolved` list of that evaluation. If the same condition holds
again later, the *same alert id* is reused and `occurrences` keeps counting.
Because the condition covers the whole window, a series that produced one bad
bucket stays unresolved until that bucket has left the window.

**Silence vs inhibition precedence.** A condition that holds and whose `for_ms`
is satisfied is first checked against active silences: a silence is active when
`starts_ms <= now_ms <= ends_ms`, the tenant matches and every silence label
matcher is present in the series labels. Inside an active silence the alert state
is `silenced` (it is *not* firing) and the silence id and reason are recorded.
Only if no silence matches is inhibition checked: an inhibition
`(source_severity, target_severity, same_labels)` marks a `target_severity` alert
as `inhibited` while an alert of at least `source_severity` is currently
`firing` in the same tenant with *exactly the same label set*. Silence therefore
wins over inhibition. A silenced or inhibited alert still counts its
`occurrences` and returns to `firing` as soon as the silence/inhibition no longer
applies. `list_alerts(state=None)` filters by `firing`, `silenced`, `inhibited`
or `resolved`.

**Notification routing.** `add_route({"tenant","target","labels"?,"severities"?,
"events"?,"repeat_ms"?,"id"?})` registers a notification route; `tenant` and
`target` are required non-empty strings, `labels` is an exact label subset the
alert's series must contain, `severities` (default: all severities) and
`events` (default: `["firing","resolved"]`, the only two allowed values) are
non-empty arrays when given, and `repeat_ms` is `null` or a non-negative
integer. Invalid shapes raise `ObsError` (HTTP `400`), a duplicate `id` is a
conflict (HTTP `409`), an unknown route is `404`; without an `id` the route is
named `route-NNNN`. Deleting a route keeps its historical notifications.

`evaluate(now_ms)` still returns only the four state lists, but every alert
transition also appends to the notification queue of each matching route
(tenant equal, route labels a subset of the series labels, alert severity in
`severities`): an alert that enters `firing` — the first time, or when
recovering from `silenced`/`inhibited` — produces one `firing` record; while
the same firing state continues a repeat is emitted only when `repeat_ms` is
set and that much time has passed since the route's last notification for the
alert; entering `resolved` produces exactly one `resolved` record. Pending
(`for_ms` not yet met), silenced and inhibited alerts never produce `firing`
records. Dedup is tracked per route, so routes notify independently. Each
record is `{"id": "notification-NNNNN","route_id","alert_id","tenant",
"target","event","created_ms","alert": <snapshot>,"acked": false}` and is
persisted across restarts together with the dedup state.
`list_notifications(tenant, route_id, alert_id, acked)` reads the queue
without consuming it; `ack_notification(id)` marks a record acknowledged,
returns the same record on a repeated ack and raises `ObsError` (HTTP `404`)
for an unknown id.

**SLO and error budget.** `set_slo(tenant, name, metric, labels,
good_comparator, threshold, target_ratio, window_ms)` defines a good-events
ratio SLO. `slo_status(name, now_ms, tenant=None)` counts every stored sample of
the matching series inside `[now_ms - window_ms, now_ms]`:

```
total          = number of samples in the window (nulls excluded)
good           = samples where compare(value, good_comparator, threshold)
bad            = total - good
ratio          = good / total                             (0.0 when total == 0)
error_budget   = max(0.0, 1 - (1 - ratio) / (1 - target_ratio))   (target_ratio < 1)
               = 1.0 if ratio >= 1.0 else 0.0              (target_ratio == 1)
burn_rate      = (bad / total) / (1 - target_ratio)        (0.0 when target_ratio >= 1 or total == 0)
met            = ratio >= target_ratio
```

`ratio` is the observed good ratio, `target_ratio ∈ (0,1]` the objective,
`burn_rate` how fast the budget is being spent relative to the allowed bad rate
(`1.0` means exactly on budget, `> 1.0` means burning too fast) and
`error_budget` the *fraction of the allowed error budget still unspent*:
`1.0` means untouched, `0.0` means exhausted or exceeded. For any `ratio` that
meets the target the two written forms of `error_budget` are identical, since
`1 - (1-ratio)/(1-target) = (ratio - target)/(1 - target)` and
`1 - ratio/target = (target - ratio)/target` are both non-negative only inside
their own regime; the first form is the one used, because it degrades sensibly
when the ratio beats the target (more budget left) instead of pinning to `0`.
With `total == 0` the ratio is `0.0`, so the budget counts as exhausted.

Examples: 9 good + 1 bad with `target_ratio = 0.9` gives `ratio = 0.9`,
`error_budget = 0.0`, `burn_rate = 0.1/0.1 = 1.0`, `met = true` (exactly on
budget). 98 good + 2 bad with `target_ratio = 0.95` gives `ratio = 0.98`,
`burn_rate = 0.02/0.05 = 0.4` and `error_budget = 1 - 0.02/0.05 = 0.6` (60% of
the budget still unspent). 90 good + 10 bad with `target_ratio = 0.99` gives
`ratio = 0.9`, `burn_rate = 10.0`, `error_budget = 0.0`, `met = false`.

**Determinism.** No module calls `time.time()` inside decision logic: `now_ms` is
passed into `evaluate`, `slo_status` and `write` (the HTTP layer uses the wall
clock only when a caller omits `now_ms` on `GET /v1/slos/status`, and
`/v1/slos/status` requires it in the CLI).

## Layout

```
obsd/__init__.py    public exports
obsd/tsdb.py        SeriesStore
obsd/alerts.py      AlertEngine
obsd/access.py      AccessControl (principals + audit log)
obsd/http_app.py    ThreadingHTTPServer + create_server
obsd/cli.py         command line interface
obsd/__main__.py    python3 -m obsd entry point
tests/              unittest suite (tsdb, alerts, http, access)
```

## Tests

```bash
python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -v
```

Covered: series identity and label-order independence, idempotent re-write,
conflicting-timestamp rejection and `overwrite`, range filtering, epoch-aligned
buckets, null buckets, all five aggregations, deterministic rollups,
sliding-window grids with left-open/right-closed windows, null empty windows
(including count), full grids for empty series and groups, window argument
